# Linear Models {#sec-intro-linear-models .unnumbered}

_Original chapter by Rafael A. Irizarry, from [*Introduction to Data Science*](https://rafalab.dfci.harvard.edu/dsbook-part-2/linear-models/intro-to-linear-models.html). Adapted by Giorgio Arcara: the examples are replaced with behavioural ones; some passages are shortened; the text is otherwise Irizarry's. Details in the [CHANGELOG](https://github.com/intro-to-behds/behdsbook-part-2/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)._

<!-- 22 Nov 2026 (Claude): part restored to the build with Ch. 15-17; the chapters on association tests and generalized linear models (Ch. 18) and on multivariable regression (Ch. 20) are still hidden, and Ch. 19 moved to Foundations of Behavioural Research. -->

Up to this point, this book has focused mainly on one variable at a time, or on the comparison of a few groups. In real data analysis, however, we are often interested in the relationship between two or more variables. In this part of the book, we introduce linear models, a general framework that unifies methods for studying associations among variables, including simple regression, regression with several predictors, and treatment effect models. Many of the tests of the *Basic Statistics* part, such as the t-test and the ANOVA, turn out to be special cases of the linear model. We use one case study throughout: whether users who are more consistent from one session to the next also engage more with an app (@sec-regression), how to take into account a variable that affects both, such as sex (@sec-adjusting-confounder), and whether a redesigned interface increases engagement in a randomised experiment (@sec-treatment-effect-models). When an association can be read as a cause is discussed in @sec-association-not-causation, in the first part of the book.
